sections.title: The organism, pathogenesis and who gets TB

blocks.text: TB is caused by **_Mycobacterium tuberculosis_ (MTB)**, one of a complex of organisms that also includes **_M. bovis_** (reservoir: cattle) and **_M. africanum_** (reservoir: humans). MTB is an **aerobic, intracellular** bacillus. Its waxy wall holds stain even after an acid wash, so it is called an **acid-fast bacillus (AFB)**. It divides very slowly, which makes it hard both to culture and to treat.

blocks.title: How infection develops
items: Spread is by **inhaled droplet nuclei** from a person with active pulmonary disease. Bacilli settle in the alveoli and recruit macrophages and lymphocytes
Macrophages turn into **epithelioid cells and Langhans giant cells**, which group with lymphocytes into the **caseating granuloma**
**Ghon focus**: the first caseous lesion, usually in the **lung periphery** (subpleural). Ghon focus + involved hilar nodes = **primary complex (of Ranke)**, also called the Ghon complex
A fibrous capsule usually walls off the primary complex, which may later **calcify** and be visible on CXR
Before immunity develops, bacilli can seed lymph nodes, serous membranes, meninges, bone, liver and kidney, and **lie dormant for years**. Control depends on **cell-mediated immunity**

blocks.text: **_M. bovis_** is caught by drinking **unpasteurised milk**, and by farmers and abattoir workers. It involves extrapulmonary sites such as lymph nodes more often. Treat it with **isoniazid, rifampicin and ethambutol**, because resistance to **pyrazinamide** is common.

blocks.title: Factors that raise the risk of TB
rows: Very young and elderly; first-generation migrants from high-prevalence countries; close contacts of smear-positive cases; overcrowding (prisons, hostels) and homelessness; drug or alcohol misuse; smoking; self-healed TB on CXR; primary infection within the past year
**HIV**; **anti-TNF** and other biologics; high-dose glucocorticoids; cytotoxic chemotherapy; transplant
Lymphoma and leukaemia; **diabetes**; **chronic kidney disease**; **silicosis**; malnutrition (including gastrectomy and jejuno-ileal bypass); vitamin D or A deficiency; recent measles in children

blocks.title: Numbers worth knowing
items: About **10%** of infected people develop disease in their lifetime, and roughly **half of that risk falls in the first 2 years** after infection
Most active TB in low-incidence countries comes from **reactivation of latent infection** when immunity wanes (HIV, immunosuppressants, diabetes, end-stage CKD, malnutrition, ageing)
Untreated HIV raises the reactivation risk to about **8–10% per year**
WHO 2014: about **9.6 million** new cases and **1.5 million** deaths. TB ranks alongside HIV as a leading infectious cause of death

blocks.text: Post-primary (reactivation) TB favours the **apex of an upper lobe** because the **higher oxygen tension** there suits this strictly aerobic organism.
Only **active pulmonary or laryngeal** TB is infectious. People with latent TB, or with extrapulmonary TB alone, do not spread it.

blocks.note: Look at: the tuberculous granuloma, with multinucleate giant cells around a central area of caseous necrosis.

sections.title: Pulmonary TB: primary, miliary and post-primary

blocks.title: Forms of pulmonary TB
rows: First infection of a tuberculin-negative person. Often silent or a flu-like illness with **skin-test conversion**. Hypersensitivity: **erythema nodosum**, phlyctenular conjunctivitis, dactylitis
**Unilateral hilar** or paratracheal nodes; collapse or consolidation, especially of the **right middle lobe**; may have a pleural effusion
Blood-borne spread. Usually **2–3 weeks** of fever, night sweats, anorexia, weight loss and dry cough; hepatosplenomegaly; headache suggests meningitis
Fine **1–2 mm 'millet seed'** nodules throughout both lungs; **choroidal tubercles** on fundoscopy; anaemia and leucopenia = marrow involvement
Over 60s; intermittent low-grade **PUO**, weight loss, debility; blood dyscrasias
**Normal CXR** and **negative TST**; diagnosis by liver or bone marrow biopsy showing granulomas or AFB
Reactivation or re-infection. **Insidious** over weeks: fever, night sweats, malaise, weight loss, cough becoming productive, haemoptysis
Ill-defined **upper-lobe** opacity that progresses to consolidation, collapse and **cavitation**. Cavitation or a miliary pattern favours active disease

blocks.title: Natural history of untreated primary infection
rows: Lymph node, gut, bone and joint disease

blocks.title: Ways pulmonary TB presents
items: Chronic cough, often with **haemoptysis**
Pyrexia of unknown origin; weight loss and general debility
Pneumonia that fails to resolve
Exudative pleural effusion
Spontaneous pneumothorax, or an incidental CXR finding in a well person

blocks.title: Complications of chronic pulmonary TB
items: Pulmonary: **massive haemoptysis**, cor pulmonale, fibrosis, **aspergilloma**, bronchiectasis, bronchopleural fistula, airflow obstruction, atypical mycobacterial infection
Non-pulmonary: **empyema necessitans**, laryngitis, **amyloidosis**, **Poncet's polyarthritis**, enteritis and anorectal disease from swallowed sputum

blocks.text: In miliary TB the **CNS is involved in about 20%**. Kumar advises brain MRI for everyone (to find a silent tuberculoma) and KC Essentials advises **lumbar puncture in all**, because meningeal spread lengthens treatment.
A **normal CXR and a negative tuberculin test do not exclude TB** in an older patient with PUO. Think of **cryptic miliary TB** and ask for liver or bone marrow biopsy.

blocks.note: Look at: the routes of spread from the primary focus: to nodes (primary complex), direct progression, to the pleura (effusion), and by blood (miliary TB, meningitis, bone and kidney).
Look at: the four CXR patterns (miliary, effusion/empyema, cavitation, consolidation/collapse) and the differential listed for each.

blocks.text: Around **70% of TB is pulmonary**. Extrapulmonary disease makes up about **20% of cases in HIV-negative patients** and is more common with HIV. Constitutional symptoms may be absent in extrapulmonary disease: about half of patients with TB lymphadenitis have none.

blocks.title: Sites of extrapulmonary TB
rows: Painless, firm cervical or supraclavicular nodes that mat together, liquefy and may discharge (**'collar-stud' abscess**, sinus)
**Cold abscess**: no overlying redness. Diagnose by ultrasound-guided FNA or core biopsy for AFB smear, culture and cytology
About half of abdominal TB. Fever, weight loss, **right iliac fossa mass**; up to 30% present as an acute abdomen
Main differential is **Crohn's disease**; diagnose on colonoscopic biopsy
Exudative ascites with **lymphocytes**; white tubercles on peritoneum at laparoscopy
Insidious breathlessness and abdominal swelling; raised JVP, pulsus paradoxus, ascites, oedema
Effusion or **constriction**; calcification in about **25%**; steroids help both forms
Chronic back pain, **lower thoracic/lumbar** spine; **psoas or cold abscess**; kyphosis; cord compression
Starts as **discitis** then spreads to anterior vertebral bodies. Malignancy usually **spares the disc**
Usually hip or knee; insidious pain and swelling
Poncet's arthropathy is a reactive polyarthritis that settles within 2 months of treatment
Headache, vomiting, cranial nerve palsy, confusion
Rapidly fatal if missed; mortality about **30% even when treated**
Frequency, dysuria, haematuria; epididymitis; female infertility

blocks.text: Exam clue: a fluctuant neck swelling in a migrant that is **not red or hot** is a **tuberculous cold abscess** until proven otherwise.
Spinal TB and vertebral metastases can look alike. TB **destroys the disc first**; malignancy attacks the **vertebral body and leaves the disc intact**.

blocks.note: Look at: the body map of extrapulmonary TB: meningitis and tuberculoma, nodes, pericardial disease, ascites, psoas abscess, kyphosis, monoarthritis and genitourinary disease.

blocks.text: Investigate any **unexplained cough lasting more than 2–3 weeks** (especially where TB is common) or typical CXR/CT changes. **Sputum smear microscopy is the key first step.** Send several samples, including an **early-morning** one; use induced sputum, bronchoscopy with lavage, or gastric washings in children if sputum cannot be produced.

blocks.title: Tests for active TB
rows: Positive smear = **presumptive** diagnosis and infectious patient
**More sensitive, less specific** than ZN; increasingly replacing it
Solid media (Löwenstein–Jensen) **4–6 weeks**; liquid media (MGIT) about **2 weeks**. Culture smear-negative samples too: only 10–100 organisms are needed
Specific but **not sensitive enough to replace culture** (Pocket: sensitivity 74%, specificity 98%)
Raised in pleural, pericardial, CSF and ascitic TB
Useful because these fluids contain few bacilli
For the very sick HIV patient with **CD4 ≤ 100 cells/μL**
Liver or bone marrow in disseminated disease; node FNA/biopsy

blocks.title: CXR patterns
items: Primary: patchy consolidation, **hilar nodes**, effusion
Post-primary: **upper-zone** patchy or nodular shadowing with **cavitation**, volume loss and fibrosis
Miliary: uniform **1–2 mm** nodules throughout the lungs (a classic spot diagnosis), although the CXR can also be normal

blocks.title: Other key points
items: A clinical response to empirical anti-TB drugs usually appears after **5–10 days**
TB PCR only helps at **first diagnosis**: it often stays positive during treatment because it detects **dead organisms**
TB CSF: lymphocytes, **low glucose**, **high protein**, high ADA
Offer every TB patient an **HIV test** (TB is AIDS-defining) and screen for hepatitis B and C
Smear-positive patients are infectious and should be **isolated**; smear-negative, culture-positive patients are much less infectious

blocks.text: The **TST and IGRA detect infection, not active disease**. In a symptomatic patient with an abnormal CXR, send sputum for AFB smear and culture; a negative skin test does not exclude TB.

In **HIV** the tuberculin response is **blunted**, sputum smear is often **negative** even in lung disease, the CXR is often atypical and disease is frequently extrapulmonary. **Culture** is the most reliable test.

Books differ on the number of sputum samples: Davidson asks for **at least two, preferably three**, including an early-morning sample; Kumar and KC Essentials say **three**. Davidson is the primary source here.

blocks.note: Look at: bilateral upper-lobe airspace shadowing with cavitation, the typical CXR of post-primary TB.
Look at: red acid-fast bacilli on a Ziehl–Neelsen stain that kept the carbol fuchsin after acid-alcohol washing.
Look at: patchy right mid- and upper-zone consolidation with a cavity at the right apex.

sections.title: Treatment, monitoring and drug adverse effects

blocks.title: Standard regimen for new, drug-sensitive TB (WHO)
rows: Kill the bulk of the bacilli quickly

blocks.title: Principles
items: Start at once if **smear-positive**, or smear-negative with typical CXR and no response to ordinary antibiotics
Daily dosing is best; **fixed-dose combination** tablets are preferred. Never treat active TB with a single drug
**12 months** for meningeal TB (including spinal TB involving the cord); KC Essentials adds **9 months for bone TB**
**Pyridoxine** prevents isoniazid neuropathy: Davidson gives it to pregnant and malnourished patients; KC Essentials gives 10 mg daily routinely
If resistance is not expected, patients can be treated as **non-infectious after 2 weeks** of correct therapy
Before starting: LFTs, creatinine, HIV and hepatitis screen, **visual acuity and colour vision**; TB is a **notifiable** disease and contacts must be traced
Keep all four drugs beyond 2 months if susceptibility results are still awaited

blocks.title: First-line drugs: action and main adverse effects
rows: **Peripheral neuropathy** (pyridoxine prevents it); **hepatitis** (more in slow acetylators and alcoholics); rash, fever; lupus-like reaction
**Orange-red urine, tears and sweat**; hepatitis; febrile reactions; thrombocytopenia; strong **CYP450 inducer**
**Retrobulbar optic neuritis**: loss of **green (red-green) colour vision**, reduced acuity, central scotoma; usually reversible if stopped early. Reduce dose in renal impairment

blocks.text: **Hepatotoxicity.** Adverse reactions occur in about **10%** of patients and more often with HIV. A mild, symptomless rise in transaminases is common, but **significant hepatitis occurs in only 2–5%**. If hepatitis develops, **stop the drugs**, let symptoms settle and LFTs recover, then **reintroduce the drugs one at a time**. Kumar gives the trigger to stop as a **rising bilirubin or transaminases above 3× normal**.

The threshold for stopping for liver toxicity varies: Kumar **> 3× normal or raised bilirubin**; Step-Up **3–5× ULN**; Pocket **5× ULN or symptoms** (for isoniazid given for latent TB); KC Essentials **only if hepatitis develops**. Davidson simply advises stopping and stepwise reintroduction.

**Rifampicin** makes the **oral contraceptive pill unreliable** and weakens anticoagulants, antiepileptics and antidepressants. It can also **unmask hypoadrenalism** by speeding glucocorticoid breakdown.

blocks.title: Monitoring, adherence and outcome
items: Repeat sputum smear at **2 and 5 months**. **Treatment failure** = positive smear or culture at **5 months**
**Still culture-positive at 2 months** raises suspicion of **MDR-TB** and is a reason to admit
**Directly observed therapy (DOT)** (supervised doses, 3 times weekly) for those unlikely to adhere: homeless people, drug or alcohol users, serious mental illness, past non-adherence, prison history
Main causes of failure: **wrong prescribing and poor adherence**
After a full course relapse risk is **under 5%**. Untreated smear-positive TB stays infectious for about **2 years**, and **25% die within a year**

blocks.title: Glucocorticoids and surgery
items: **Steroids recommended** for **pericardial and meningeal TB**, and for children with endobronchial disease; may help ureteric TB, pleural effusion and extensive lung disease
**Surgery**, usually after a full drug course, for massive haemoptysis, loculated empyema, constrictive pericarditis, suppurating nodes, or spinal disease with cord compression

blocks.text: **TB with HIV:** rifampicin lowers protease inhibitor levels, so **rifabutin** (a weaker inducer) can be used instead. Give **at least 2 weeks** of TB treatment before starting ART, and expect possible **IRIS** (paradoxical worsening) once ART starts.
Classic exam question: a patient has just started rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide and ethambutol; what else should be prescribed? **Pyridoxine (vitamin B6).**

sections.title: Latent TB: skin test, IGRA, chemoprophylaxis and BCG

blocks.text: **Latent TB infection (LTBI)**: the immune system holds a small number of dormant bacilli in check. There are **no symptoms, the CXR is normal and the person is not infectious**, but the infection can reactivate later. Lifetime risk of disease is about **5–15%**, mostly within **5 years** of infection. LTBI is diagnosed by showing **immune memory** to mycobacterial antigens with a **TST or an IGRA**.

blocks.title: Contact tracing
items: Evidence of infection is found in about **10–20%** of close contacts of **smear-positive** pulmonary TB
and in only **2–5%** of contacts of **smear-negative, culture-positive** disease
KC Essentials: if the first skin test of a contact is negative, **repeat it at 6 weeks**; Step-Up repeats **8–10 weeks** after the last exposure

blocks.title: Tuberculin skin test (Mantoux) versus IGRA
rows: PPD injected **intradermally** on the inner forearm; read at **48–72 h**
Blood T cells exposed to **ESAT-6 and CFP-10**; IFN-γ measured (QuantiFERON or T-SPOT.TB)
Measure **induration (not redness)** across the forearm; Davidson/NICE: **≥ 5 mm positive**
**More specific**: antigens not shared with BCG or most other mycobacteria
**People with HIV**; UK dual strategy is TST then IGRA
Cannot separate **latent from active** TB; may be indeterminate if immunosuppressed

blocks.title: Why a skin test misleads
rows: Booster effect from an earlier skin test
**Active or overwhelming TB**; very recent infection (takes 2–10 weeks to convert)

blocks.text: TST cut-offs differ by source. Davidson (and NICE, per Zero to Finals) call **≥ 5 mm** positive; KC Essentials uses **≥ 10 mm**; US books stratify: **≥ 5 mm** in HIV, transplant, close contacts or old TB on CXR, **≥ 10 mm** in other high-risk groups, **≥ 15 mm** with no risk factors. Follow Davidson.

blocks.title: Who is offered LTBI treatment
items: Asymptomatic contacts with a positive test and a **normal CXR**; Davidson offers this to adults up to **65**
Household and close workplace contacts of **pulmonary or laryngeal** TB; health workers; recent migrants from high-incidence countries
**HIV** (consider for HIV-positive close contacts of smear-positive TB)
Before **biologics such as infliximab**, and before stem-cell or solid-organ transplant
Old TB on CXR in someone about to start immunosuppression

blocks.title: Chemoprophylaxis regimens
rows: **Isoniazid + rifampicin for 3 months**, or **isoniazid alone for 6 months**
Rifampicin alone 4 months; isoniazid + rifapentine weekly for 12 weeks; isoniazid 6–9 months with pyridoxine
No proven regimen: refer to a specialist

blocks.text: **Exclude active TB before treating latent TB** (symptom review, examination, CXR); otherwise a single- or two-drug course could breed resistance. Treating a positive skin test cuts lifetime risk from about **10% to 1%**.

blocks.title: BCG vaccine
items: **Live attenuated** strain derived from _M. bovis_, given **intradermally**
Protects **children against disseminated TB and TB meningitis**; protection in adults is inconsistent
**Contraindicated** in the immunocompromised (e.g. HIV) and in **pregnancy**
Causes a positive Mantoux; check the skin test is negative before giving it

blocks.note: Look at: the Mantoux injection on the inner forearm and how the indurated area is measured across the arm (positive when ≥ 5 mm).
Look at: the two IGRA formats: T-SPOT.TB counts IFN-γ spots from purified T cells; QuantiFERON measures IFN-γ in whole-blood supernatant.

blocks.title: Definitions
rows: MDR **plus any fluoroquinolone** **plus at least one injectable** second-line drug (amikacin, kanamycin or capreomycin)

blocks.title: Size of the problem
items: MDR-TB affects about **3.3% of new** cases and **20% of previously treated** cases worldwide
About **9.7%** of MDR-TB is XDR-TB; MDR-TB caused about 190 000 deaths in 2014
Rising most in the former Soviet Union, Central Asia and Africa; commoner with **HIV** and after **inadequate earlier treatment**

blocks.title: Why resistance appears, and whom to suspect
columns: Risk factors in a patient (Kumar, Pocket)
rows: **Previous TB treatment**, especially unsupervised or with poor adherence
Infection acquired in a **high-resistance region** (e.g. India, China, Eastern Europe/Russia, South Africa)
Contact with a known **resistant case**; exposed health workers
**No response despite good adherence**; advanced HIV with prior treatment; repeated **fluoroquinolone** courses for presumed pneumonia

blocks.text: Mutations giving **rifampicin resistance strongly predict MDR-TB**. Xpert MTB/RIF detects them in **under 2 hours**, so resistant TB can be treated long before culture sensitivities return.

blocks.title: Management
items: Resistance is acquired through **incomplete or incorrect treatment** and can then be **transmitted**
Cure is possible but needs **prolonged** treatment with drugs that are **less effective, more toxic and more expensive**; KC Essentials quotes up to **2 years** of sensitivity-guided combinations
Refer to a specialist; mortality is high for MDR-TB and higher still for XDR-TB

blocks.text: XDR wording varies: Davidson says resistance to **any quinolone** plus one injectable; Kumar says **high-level** fluoroquinolone resistance and names amikacin, capreomycin or kanamycin; KC Essentials uses the vague label 'EDR'. Learn Davidson's definition.

TB is one of the **common causes of pleural effusion**. Tuberculous pleurisy follows spread of infection to the pleura, where granuloma breakdown and local inflammation produce the fluid. It typically appears **3–6 months after primary infection**, though it can also complicate reactivation. It may coexist with pericardial and peritoneal effusions. Kumar notes that **pleuritic pain** is a frequent presenting complaint when the pleura is involved.

blocks.title: Tuberculous pleural fluid
rows: **Raised**. Pocket: > 70 suggests TB, < 40 makes TB unlikely
Positive in about **80%** (Davidson): the best single test

blocks.title: Light's criteria: exudate if any one is met
items: Pleural/serum **protein** ratio **> 0.5**
Pleural/serum **LDH** ratio **> 0.6**
Pleural LDH **> two-thirds** of the upper limit of normal serum LDH

blocks.title: Management
items: A TB effusion often settles by itself, but the patient **still needs a full course of treatment for active TB**
Glucocorticoids **may** help pleural effusions (not routinely required)
Do **not drain to dryness** before a diagnosis is made, because it can prevent a pleural biopsy
TB is, with bacterial pneumonia, a common cause of **empyema**; telling tuberculous from other empyema may need pleural biopsy with histology, culture and/or NAAT

blocks.text: A **lymphocyte-predominant exudate** should make you think of **TB** (and malignancy).

Yields differ between books. Davidson: fluid culture **20%**, biopsy **80%**. Pocket: fluid AFB stain 0–10%, culture 11–50%, biopsy about 70%. Both agree that **biopsy beats fluid**. Davidson also says about **200 mL** shows on a PA CXR; Kumar says 300 mL on X-ray and 500 mL clinically.

cards.front: Which mycobacteria make up the _M. tuberculosis_ complex mentioned by Davidson, and their reservoirs?
cards.back: _M. tuberculosis_; _M. bovis_ (cattle); _M. africanum_ (humans)

cards.front: What is the Ghon focus, and what is the primary complex?
cards.back: Ghon focus: peripheral caseous primary lung lesion. Ghon focus + involved hilar nodes = primary complex (of Ranke)

cards.front: Why does post-primary TB favour the lung apex?
cards.back: Higher oxygen tension there suits the strictly aerobic organism

cards.front: Lifetime risk of disease after primary TB infection?
cards.back: About 10%, with roughly half of it in the first 2 years

cards.front: Classic CXR of primary TB?
cards.back: Unilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, with collapse/consolidation especially of the right middle lobe

cards.front: Features of cryptic miliary TB?
cards.back: Age > 60, low-grade PUO, weight loss, normal CXR, negative TST; diagnosed by liver or marrow biopsy

cards.front: What eye finding supports miliary TB?
cards.back: Choroidal tubercles on fundoscopy

cards.front: Commonest extrapulmonary site of TB?
cards.back: Lymph nodes (cervical and mediastinal most often)

cards.front: How does spinal TB differ from vertebral malignancy on imaging?
cards.back: TB starts as discitis and destroys the disc; malignancy usually spares the disc

cards.front: Which TB smear stain is more sensitive but less specific than Ziehl–Neelsen?
cards.back: Auramine (fluorescent) staining

cards.front: Time to culture MTB on solid vs liquid media?
cards.back: Solid: 4–6 weeks; liquid (MGIT): about 2 weeks

cards.front: What does Xpert MTB/RIF detect, and how fast?
cards.back: MTB DNA and rifampicin-resistance mutations, in under 2 hours

cards.front: Standard regimen for new drug-sensitive pulmonary TB?
cards.back: 2 months HRZE, then 4 months HR (6 months total)

cards.front: Which TB drug causes loss of green colour vision, and what is checked first?
cards.back: Ethambutol (retrobulbar neuritis). Check Snellen acuity and Ishihara colour vision

cards.front: Total treatment length for TB meningitis?
cards.back: 12 months (with adjuvant glucocorticoids)

cards.front: How is TB treatment failure defined?
cards.back: Positive sputum smear or culture at 5 months

cards.front: What is a positive Mantoux in Davidson?
cards.back: Induration ≥ 5 mm measured across the forearm at 48–72 h

cards.front: Why is an IGRA more specific than the TST?
cards.back: Its antigens (ESAT-6, CFP-10) are not shared with BCG or most other mycobacteria

cards.front: Davidson's chemoprophylaxis regimens for latent TB?
cards.back: Isoniazid + rifampicin for 3 months, or isoniazid alone for 6 months

cards.front: Two groups who must not receive BCG?
cards.back: The immunocompromised (e.g. HIV) and pregnant women

cards.front: Define MDR-TB and XDR-TB.
cards.back: MDR: resistant to at least rifampicin and isoniazid. XDR: MDR plus any quinolone plus ≥ 1 injectable second-line drug

cards.front: Which single resistance mutation strongly predicts MDR-TB?
cards.back: Rifampicin resistance

cards.front: Davidson's yields in tuberculous pleural effusion?
cards.back: Fluid culture about 20%; pleural biopsy about 80%

cards.front: Light's criteria for an exudate?
cards.back: Protein ratio > 0.5, LDH ratio > 0.6, or pleural LDH > two-thirds of the upper limit of serum LDH (any one)

questions.leadIn: Pick the best-fitting option for each patient. An option may fit one patient, several patients or none.
options: Close household contact with smear-positive TB

items.stem: A 47-year-old dairy farmer has a 3-month history of a painless swelling in the neck. Node biopsy shows caseating granulomas. The mycobacterium cultured is **resistant to pyrazinamide**. He and his family drink milk straight from his own herd.
items.explanation: Pyrazinamide resistance and lymph-node disease point to **_M. bovis_**, which is caught from **unpasteurised milk** from infected cattle (and by farm and abattoir workers).

items.stem: A 61-year-old man spent 30 years sandblasting in a foundry. His CXR has shown small upper-zone nodules and fibrosis for years, put down to his work. He now has weight loss and a new cavity; sputum is AFB-positive.
items.explanation: Long exposure to silica dust with nodular upper-zone fibrosis means **silicosis**, which Davidson lists as a disease that raises TB risk.

items.stem: A 35-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis started infliximab 4 months ago without any TB screening. She now has 3 weeks of fever and night sweats, and her CXR shows diffuse tiny nodules.
items.explanation: Davidson lists **anti-TNF and other biologic therapies** among the immunosuppressive causes of TB, and latent infection can reactivate once they start. This is why people are screened for latent TB **before anti-TNF therapy**.

questions.leadIn: Pick the best-fitting option for each patient. An option may fit one patient, several patients or none.

items.stem: A 7-year-old girl has had a mild flu-like illness and tender red nodules on both shins. Six weeks ago her grandfather was diagnosed with smear-positive TB. Her CXR shows **unilateral hilar lymphadenopathy** and her skin test has just turned positive.
items.explanation: A recent first infection with **skin-test conversion**, a hypersensitivity sign (**erythema nodosum**) and unilateral hilar nodes is **primary TB**.

items.stem: A 74-year-old man has had intermittent low-grade fever and weight loss for 4 months. He is pancytopenic. His **CXR is normal** and his **tuberculin test is negative**. A bone marrow biopsy shows granulomas containing acid-fast bacilli.
items.explanation: Old age, PUO, a normal CXR and a negative TST, with diagnosis on marrow biopsy, is the textbook picture of **cryptic miliary TB**.

items.stem: A 29-year-old woman has 3 weeks of fever, night sweats, dry cough and a new headache. Fundoscopy shows small pale lesions in the choroid. Her CXR shows countless 1–2 mm nodules in both lungs.
items.explanation: Diffuse **1–2 mm 'millet seed'** nodules plus **choroidal tubercles** mean blood-borne (miliary) spread. The headache should prompt a search for TB meningitis, present in about 20%.

items.stem: A 46-year-old homeless man with alcohol dependence has 2 months of weight loss, night sweats and a cough now producing blood-streaked sputum. CXR shows right upper lobe consolidation with a cavity.
items.explanation: An insidious illness with **upper-lobe cavitation** in an adult with social risk factors is **post-primary TB**, which favours the oxygen-rich apex.

questions.leadIn: Pick the best-fitting option for each patient. An option may fit one patient, several patients or none.

items.stem: A 30-year-old woman who moved from Somalia 2 years ago has a painless neck lump that has grown slowly for 5 months. It is now fluctuant, with **no overlying redness or warmth**, and has started to discharge through the skin.
items.explanation: A slowly enlarging, painless node that liquefies and discharges without inflammation is a **cold abscess** ('collar-stud') of **tuberculous lymphadenitis**, the commonest extrapulmonary site.

items.stem: A 52-year-old man from Pakistan has months of urinary frequency, dysuria and microscopic haematuria. Repeated urine samples show many white cells but **no growth** on routine culture. He has no fever.
items.explanation: **Sterile pyuria** with lower urinary symptoms and little systemic upset fits **renal tract TB**. Urine should be sent for mycobacterial culture.

items.stem: A 41-year-old man from India has 3 months of low back pain and evening fevers. MRI shows destruction of the **L1/L2 disc** with erosion of the front of both vertebral bodies and a collection tracking along the psoas.
items.explanation: Infection that starts in the **disc**, spreads to the anterior vertebral bodies and forms a **psoas abscess** is **Pott's disease**. Malignancy usually leaves the disc intact.

items.stem: A 38-year-old woman has slowly worsening breathlessness and abdominal swelling. She has a raised JVP, pulsus paradoxus, ascites and leg oedema. Her CXR shows a **rim of calcification around the heart**; she was treated for TB in childhood.
items.explanation: Raised JVP, ascites and oedema with **pericardial calcification** (seen in about 25%) means **tuberculous constrictive pericarditis**. Surgery may be needed for constriction.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man who moved from Bangladesh last year has had a cough for 5 weeks, with evening fevers and 5 kg weight loss. His CXR shows patchy right upper-zone shadowing with a small cavity. He can expectorate sputum.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate first investigation?
options: Sputum smear for acid-fast bacilli on at least two samples, including an early-morning one
questions.explanation: Davidson calls **sputum smear microscopy the most important first step**: at least two (preferably three) samples, one early in the morning. Samples also go for culture, which confirms the diagnosis and gives drug sensitivities.
whyNot: A TST shows infection, not active disease, and has low sensitivity and specificity for active TB.
An IGRA cannot tell active from latent TB, so it does not answer the question in a symptomatic patient.
Nothing here suggests pulmonary embolism; a cavity with constitutional symptoms points to TB.
Bronchoscopy is kept for patients who cannot produce sputum or whose smears are unhelpful.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old woman from Pakistan has 2 months of abdominal swelling, low-grade fever and weight loss. Ascitic fluid is an exudate with mostly lymphocytes. The AFB smear of the fluid is negative and culture has been sent.
questions.leadIn: Which additional test on the fluid best supports tuberculosis while culture is awaited?
questions.explanation: T-cell activation by mycobacterial antigens raises **adenosine deaminase** in ascitic, pleural, pericardial and CSF fluid. Body fluids contain few bacilli, so smear is often negative and ADA helps while culture grows.
whyNot: Amylase points to pancreatic disease, not TB.
A high triglyceride level suggests chylous ascites.
The albumin gradient separates portal-hypertensive from other ascites but does not point to TB.
Gram stain looks for ordinary bacteria; mycobacteria need acid-fast or fluorescent stains.

questions.leadIn: Pick the best-fitting option for each patient. An option may fit one patient, several patients or none.

items.stem: A 50-year-old malnourished man with alcohol dependence develops burning pain and numbness in both feet 6 weeks into quadruple TB therapy. No vitamin supplement was prescribed.
items.explanation: **Isoniazid** causes peripheral neuropathy by interfering with pyridoxine (vitamin B6). Davidson gives **pyridoxine** to pregnant and malnourished patients to prevent it, and KC Essentials gives it routinely.

items.stem: A 26-year-old woman taking the combined oral contraceptive pill becomes pregnant 2 months after starting TB treatment. She also mentions her contact lenses have turned orange.
items.explanation: **Rifampicin** induces liver enzymes, so the pill fails; it also stains tears, urine and sweat orange-red.

items.stem: A 58-year-old man in the intensive phase of treatment develops a hot, swollen first MTP joint. His serum urate is high.
items.explanation: **Pyrazinamide** reduces renal urate excretion and can cause hyperuricaemia and **gout**. Step-Up notes ethambutol can occasionally precipitate gout too, but pyrazinamide is the classic cause.

items.stem: A 44-year-old woman 3 months into treatment says that green objects look grey and her reading is blurred. Ishihara plates show new errors.
items.explanation: **Ethambutol** causes a dose-related **retrobulbar optic neuritis** with loss of green colour vision and reduced acuity. It usually recovers if the drug is stopped early.

items.stem: A 33-year-old man being treated for TB meningitis received a first-line injectable drug in place of ethambutol. He now has tinnitus, unsteadiness and reduced hearing.
items.explanation: In meningeal TB, Davidson notes ethambutol may be replaced by **streptomycin**, an aminoglycoside that damages the **8th cranial nerve**. Spotting the drug substitution is the two-step part.

questions.theme: Screening and management of latent TB
questions.leadIn: Pick the best-fitting option for each patient. An option may fit one patient, several patients or none.

items.stem: A 31-year-old nurse with well-controlled **HIV** is a close contact of a colleague with smear-positive TB. She is well. Which test should be used first to look for infection?
items.explanation: In the UK an **IGRA is the first-choice test in people with HIV**, whose skin-test responses are blunted and unreliable.

items.stem: An 8-year-old boy is a household contact of his uncle, who has smear-positive pulmonary TB. He is well. Which test should be used first?
items.explanation: Davidson: the **TST remains the first choice in children**.

items.stem: A 56-year-old man with a mechanical mitral valve on warfarin is a household contact of a smear-positive case. He is well, his IGRA is positive and his CXR is normal.
items.explanation: He needs chemoprophylaxis. **Rifampicin induces liver enzymes and weakens warfarin**, so **isoniazid alone for 6 months** avoids the interaction.

items.stem: A 40-year-old man is screened because his wife has smear-positive TB. His IGRA is positive, but he admits 3 weeks of productive cough and his CXR shows right apical cavitation.
items.explanation: Abnormal CXR and symptoms mean **possible active TB**, which must be excluded before any latent-TB treatment. Send sputum for smear and culture.

questions.stem: A 39-year-old man who stopped his previous TB treatment early 3 years ago now has a new cavitating lesion. His sputum is smear-positive, and Xpert MTB/RIF detects a **rifampicin-resistance mutation**.
questions.leadIn: Which resistance pattern is most likely?
options: Resistance to both rifampicin and isoniazid
questions.explanation: Rifampicin-resistance mutations **strongly predict MDR-TB** (resistance to rifampicin and isoniazid). Previous incomplete treatment is the main risk factor, so treat as resistant TB pending full sensitivities.
whyNot: Pyrazinamide resistance is typical of _M. bovis_ and is not what Xpert detects.
Ethambutol resistance is not signalled by the rifampicin probe.
Streptomycin resistance alone does not explain a rifampicin mutation.
Fluoroquinolone resistance is an XDR feature and is not shown by this test.

questions.stem: Drug-sensitivity testing on a culture from a 45-year-old man shows resistance to **rifampicin, isoniazid, moxifloxacin and amikacin**.
questions.leadIn: How is this organism classified?
questions.explanation: **XDR-TB** = MDR (rifampicin + isoniazid) **plus** a quinolone **plus** at least one injectable second-line drug such as amikacin. All three conditions are met.
whyNot: MDR-TB needs only rifampicin and isoniazid resistance; quinolone plus injectable resistance upgrades it to XDR.
There is resistance to more than isoniazid.
There is resistance to more than rifampicin.
Resistance to first-line drugs rules this out.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man from Nepal has 3 weeks of fever, sweats and right-sided pleuritic pain. CXR shows a moderate right effusion. Aspirated fluid is amber. Fluid/serum protein ratio is 0.7, lymphocytes are 85% of cells, ADA is raised, and the AFB smear is negative.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: An amber **lymphocytic exudate** with **raised ADA** in a young man from a high-incidence country is **tuberculous pleurisy**. A negative smear is usual because pleural fluid holds few bacilli.
whyNot: Parapneumonic effusions are neutrophil-predominant.
Cardiac failure gives a transudate (protein ratio < 0.5).
Infarction usually gives blood-stained fluid with red cells and a source of embolism.
Pancreatic effusions have high amylase and no particular cell predominance.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman has a lymphocytic exudative pleural effusion. TB is suspected, but two fluid samples are smear-negative.
questions.leadIn: Which test has the highest diagnostic yield for tuberculous pleurisy?
options: Pleural biopsy for histology and culture
questions.explanation: Davidson: pleural **biopsy is positive in about 80%**, against about 20% for fluid culture. Pocket agrees that biopsy beats fluid tests.
whyNot: Fluid culture is positive in only about 20% (Davidson).
Smear of pleural fluid rarely shows bacilli (0–10% in Pocket).
A TST shows infection, not pleural disease, and may be negative early.
Cytology looks for malignant cells; it does not confirm TB.

questions.leadIn: Pick the best-fitting option for each patient. An option may fit one patient, several patients or none.

items.stem: A 36-year-old man with advanced HIV (CD4 60 cells/μL) is very unwell with fever and hypotension. He cannot produce sputum. A quick bedside test is wanted.
items.explanation: Davidson: the **lateral-flow urinary LAM** assay helps in the **severely ill HIV patient with CD4 ≤ 100**.

items.stem: A 40-year-old woman has a smear-positive sputum. The team needs the **definitive diagnosis and a full drug-sensitivity profile**.
items.explanation: Smear gives only a presumptive diagnosis. **Culture** is the gold standard for confirmation and phenotypic sensitivities.

items.stem: A 33-year-old man from Eastern Europe has a cavitating lesion. The clinician wants to know within **2 hours** whether TB is present and whether **rifampicin resistance** is likely.
items.explanation: **Xpert MTB/RIF** detects MTB and rifampicin-resistance mutations in under 2 hours.

items.stem: A 69-year-old woman has 3 months of low-grade fever and weight loss. Blood count shows pancytopenia. CXR is normal and her tuberculin test is negative.
items.explanation: This is the pattern of **cryptic miliary TB** (two-step: recognise it, then choose the test). Diagnosis comes from **bone marrow** (or liver) biopsy showing granulomas or AFB.

questions.stem: A 37-year-old man with untreated HIV has smear-positive cavitating pulmonary TB. A tuberculin skin test read at 72 hours shows **no induration**.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely explanation for the skin test result?
options: Booster effect from an earlier skin test
questions.explanation: HIV and other immunosuppression cause **false-negative (anergic)** skin tests; overwhelming active TB can do the same. Never use a negative TST to rule out TB.
whyNot: BCG causes false-**positive** results.
Non-tuberculous mycobacteria also cause false-**positive** results.
The booster effect increases, not abolishes, a later reaction.
The test is read between 48 and 72 hours, so 72 hours is correct timing.

questions.stem: A 49-year-old woman has been on HRZE for 3 weeks. She develops nausea and jaundice. ALT is 6 times the upper limit of normal and bilirubin is rising.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate action?
options: Stop the drugs, let the liver tests recover, then reintroduce the drugs one at a time
Continue all drugs and recheck liver tests in a month
Stop pyrazinamide permanently and continue the other three drugs
questions.explanation: This is drug-induced **hepatitis** (rising bilirubin, ALT well above 3× normal). Davidson and Kumar advise **stopping**, allowing recovery, then **stepwise reintroduction** of each drug to find the culprit.
whyNot: Continuing risks fulminant liver failure; she has symptomatic hepatitis, not a mild rise.
Isoniazid and rifampicin are also hepatotoxic, so the culprit is not known yet.
Single-drug treatment of active TB breeds resistance.
Pyridoxine prevents isoniazid neuropathy, not hepatitis.

questions.stem: A 23-year-old man is diagnosed with **tuberculous meningitis**. The organism is fully sensitive.
questions.leadIn: What total duration of antituberculous treatment is recommended?
questions.explanation: Davidson: **12 months** for meningeal TB (including spinal TB involving the cord), with adjuvant **glucocorticoids**. Most other forms need 6 months.
whyNot: 6 months is enough for pulmonary and most extrapulmonary TB, but not meningitis.
KC Essentials uses 9 months for bone TB, not meningitis.
Longer than recommended for drug-sensitive CNS disease.
Up to 2 years is the kind of duration used for drug-resistant TB.

questions.stem: A TB clinic reviews five newly diagnosed patients with drug-sensitive pulmonary TB.
questions.leadIn: Which patient is the strongest candidate for directly observed therapy?
options: A homeless man with alcohol dependence
A pregnant woman who attends every appointment
A 20-year-old student living with her parents
questions.explanation: **DOT** is for people unlikely to adhere: the **homeless**, drug or alcohol users, those with serious mental illness, and those with past non-adherence.
whyNot: Smear status does not decide DOT; adherence risk does.
Pregnancy needs pyridoxine, but she shows good adherence.
Diabetes raises TB risk but is not a DOT criterion.
Nothing suggests poor adherence.

questions.stem: A 42-year-old man started standard HRZE for smear-positive pulmonary TB. He says he has taken every dose. At **2 months** his sputum culture is **still positive**.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate interpretation?
options: Expected finding; move to the continuation phase as planned
Raises suspicion of multidrug-resistant TB; admit and obtain drug sensitivities
Meets the definition of treatment failure; stop all drugs
Shows non-adherence; start directly observed therapy only
questions.explanation: Step 1: sputum is checked at 2 and 5 months to assess response. Step 2: Davidson lists **culture-positive after 2 months** as a marker of significant **MDR-TB** risk and a reason to consider admission. Step 3: treatment failure is only defined at **5 months** (positive smear or culture). So obtain rapid molecular and culture sensitivities, and do not switch to HR blindly.
whyNot: Dropping to two drugs while resistance is possible risks amplifying it.
Failure is defined at 5 months, not 2.
He reports full adherence; resistance must be excluded first, though DOT may be added.
Neuropathy is irrelevant to a positive culture.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old man from Somalia has a left pleural effusion. Results: pleural protein 46 g/L, serum protein 70 g/L; pleural LDH 310 U/L, serum LDH 400 U/L. The fluid is amber with 90% lymphocytes, and ADA is high.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: Step 1, Light's criteria: protein ratio 46/70 = 0.66 (> 0.5) and LDH ratio 310/400 = 0.78 (> 0.6), so this is an **exudate**. Step 2, cells: **lymphocyte-predominant**. Step 3: amber fluid, raised ADA and origin in a high-incidence country point to **TB**. Confirm with **pleural biopsy** (about 80% yield) and give a full course of treatment.
whyNot: Heart failure gives a transudate.
Hypoproteinaemia gives a transudate.
Parapneumonic exudates are neutrophil-predominant.
Pancreatic effusions have high amylase and no lymphocyte predominance.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old woman shares a flat with a man just diagnosed with smear-positive pulmonary TB. She feels well and takes no medicines. Her IGRA is positive and her CXR is normal.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate management?
options: Six months of four-drug then two-drug treatment
Repeat the IGRA in a year
questions.explanation: Step 1: positive IGRA = infection. Step 2: no symptoms and a normal CXR = **latent**, not active, TB. Step 3: she is a close contact under 65, so offer **chemoprophylaxis**: Davidson gives **3 months of isoniazid + rifampicin** or 6 months of isoniazid. Warn her that rifampicin weakens hormonal contraception.
whyNot: Full treatment is for active disease, which has been excluded.
BCG is not given to someone already infected and does not treat infection.
Latent TB carries a 5–15% lifetime risk; treatment is offered to close contacts.
Repeating the test leaves her untreated and adds nothing.

questions.leadIn: Pick the best-fitting option for each patient. An option may fit one patient, several patients or none.

items.stem: A 63-year-old man treated for TB 20 years ago has had recurrent small haemoptyses. CXR shows a rounded opacity sitting inside an old left upper-lobe cavity. Serum _Aspergillus_ precipitins are positive.
items.explanation: A fungal ball growing in a **residual TB cavity** is an **aspergilloma**, a listed complication of chronic pulmonary TB.

items.stem: A 47-year-old man with untreated tuberculous empyema develops a soft, fluctuant swelling on his chest wall that begins to discharge pus.
items.explanation: Pus under pressure tracking through the chest wall to the skin is **empyema necessitans**.

items.stem: A 58-year-old woman has had poorly treated fibrocavitary TB for many years. She now has heavy proteinuria and ankle oedema, and her serum albumin is low.
items.explanation: Two-step: chronic infection such as TB drives **reactive (AA) amyloidosis**, and about 90% of patients present with proteinuria or **nephrotic syndrome**.

items.stem: A 31-year-old man with active pulmonary TB has pain and swelling in several joints. Joint fluid grows no organisms, and the arthritis settles within 2 months of starting TB treatment.
items.explanation: **Poncet's arthropathy** is an immune-mediated reactive polyarthritis linked to TB, not joint infection, and resolves with treatment.

questions.theme: Chest X-ray patterns and their differential diagnosis
questions.leadIn: Pick the best-fitting option for each patient. An option may fit one patient, several patients or none.

items.stem: A 48-year-old man has nasal crusting, haematuria with red-cell casts and a positive ANCA. CXR shows several cavitating nodules. Sputum smears and cultures for AFB are negative.
items.explanation: Cavitation has a differential (Fig. 17.37). Upper and lower airway disease with glomerulonephritis and ANCA means **granulomatosis with polyangiitis**.

items.stem: A 66-year-old retired coal miner has large conglomerate masses in both upper zones, one with central cavitation. Repeated sputum smears and cultures for mycobacteria are negative.
items.explanation: Large upper-zone conglomerate masses after coal dust exposure that can cavitate are **progressive massive fibrosis**, a listed mimic of cavitating TB. Simple coal workers' pneumoconiosis gives only small nodules.

items.stem: A 26-year-old man from Bangladesh has 5 weeks of fever, night sweats and cough. CXR shows bilateral upper-lobe shadowing with cavities, and his sputum smear is AFB-positive.
items.explanation: Upper-lobe cavitation with AFB in sputum is **post-primary TB**.

questions.stem: A 33-year-old woman is diagnosed with miliary TB on CXR and a transbronchial biopsy. She has no headache and her neurological examination is normal.
questions.leadIn: Which further investigation does Kumar recommend for every patient with miliary TB?
questions.explanation: The **CNS is involved in about 20%** of miliary TB. Kumar advises **brain MRI** in all, because a tuberculoma can be silent. KC Essentials also advises lumbar puncture, as CNS involvement extends treatment to 12 months.
whyNot: Gut TB is not routinely looked for without symptoms.
Pericardial disease is sought only if there are signs.
Bone imaging is not part of routine miliary work-up.
Renal TB is usually a late, separate presentation.

questions.stem: A community TB nurse is planning a BCG programme.
questions.leadIn: In which person is BCG vaccination contraindicated?
options: A tuberculin-negative newborn in a high-incidence area
A tuberculin-negative child who recently migrated from a high-prevalence country
questions.explanation: BCG is a **live attenuated** vaccine, so it must not be given to the **immunocompromised (e.g. HIV)** or in **pregnancy**.
whyNot: Infants in high-risk areas are a target group.
Unvaccinated health workers at occupational risk can be offered BCG.
Unvaccinated new migrants from high-prevalence countries are offered BCG.
Veterinary staff are listed as an occupational-risk group.

questions.stem: A 39-year-old man with HIV is taking a protease-inhibitor-based antiretroviral regimen. He is diagnosed with drug-sensitive pulmonary TB.
questions.leadIn: Which change to standard TB treatment is most appropriate?
options: Stop antiretroviral therapy until TB treatment ends
questions.explanation: Rifampicin is a strong **CYP450 inducer** and lowers protease-inhibitor levels, risking HIV treatment failure and resistance. **Rifabutin** induces CYP450 less and can be substituted, with dose adjustment.
whyNot: The interaction is with rifampicin, not isoniazid.
Pyrazinamide is not the problem and is needed for a 6-month course.
Stopping ART for months raises the risk of further opportunistic infection.
Single-drug treatment of active TB breeds resistance.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man from Nepal has 4 months of thoracolumbar back pain, night sweats and weight loss. MRI shows destruction of the **T12–L1 disc** with erosion of the front of both adjacent vertebral bodies and a paravertebral collection.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Disease that **begins in the disc** and spreads to the anterior vertebral bodies with an abscess, in a man from a high-incidence country, is **Pott's disease**. Malignancy targets the vertebral body and leaves the disc alone.
whyNot: Metastases usually spare the disc space.
Myeloma causes lytic lesions in the vertebral body without disc destruction or abscess.
An osteoporotic fracture does not destroy the disc or form a collection.
Ankylosing spondylitis causes stiffness and syndesmophytes, not disc destruction with abscess.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old man from India has 2 months of fever, weight loss and a tender mass in the right iliac fossa. Colonoscopy shows ulceration of the caecum. Biopsies show **caseating granulomas with acid-fast bacilli**.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Ileocaecal disease makes up about half of abdominal TB and presents with fever, weight loss and a right iliac fossa mass. **Caseation with AFB** separates it from **Crohn's disease**, its main differential.
whyNot: Crohn's granulomas are non-caseating and contain no AFB.
Carcinoma shows malignant cells, not granulomas.
An appendix abscess would not show caseating granulomas with AFB.
Ulcerative colitis starts in the rectum and does not form granulomas.

questions.stem: A TB service audits treatment outcomes for patients with pulmonary TB.
questions.leadIn: Which finding defines treatment failure?
options: Positive sputum smear or culture at 5 months
A mild, symptomless rise in transaminases
questions.explanation: In Davidson, **treatment failure** means the sputum smear or culture is **still positive at 5 months**; isolating an MDR strain also counts as failure.
whyNot: Smears are often still positive early; response is assessed at 2 and 5 months.
Symptoms can lag behind microbiological response.
Scarring often persists after cure.
Mild transaminase rises are common and not a sign of failure.

questions.leadIn: Pick the best-fitting option for each patient. An option may fit one patient, several patients or none.
options: 12 months of treatment with adjuvant glucocorticoids
6 months of treatment with adjuvant glucocorticoids

items.stem: A 22-year-old woman has headache, fever and neck stiffness. CSF shows lymphocytes, low glucose, high protein and raised ADA. Xpert on CSF detects fully sensitive MTB.
items.explanation: **TB meningitis** needs **12 months** of treatment with adjuvant **glucocorticoids**.

items.stem: A 46-year-old man has breathlessness, raised JVP and a large pericardial effusion. Pericardial fluid ADA is high and culture grows sensitive MTB.
items.explanation: Most extrapulmonary TB needs 6 months, but **pericardial TB** is one of the forms where **glucocorticoids are recommended**.

items.stem: A 52-year-old abattoir worker has tuberculous cervical lymphadenitis. The organism is identified as _M. bovis_.
items.explanation: Two-step: _M. bovis_ is commonly **resistant to pyrazinamide**, so treat with **isoniazid, rifampicin and ethambutol**.

items.stem: A 35-year-old man has newly diagnosed smear-positive pulmonary TB. Xpert shows no rifampicin resistance and he has no other illnesses.
items.explanation: New, drug-sensitive pulmonary TB: **2HRZE then 4HR**.

ospe.identify: Tuberculous granuloma: multinucleate (Langhans) giant cells and epithelioid macrophages around central **caseous necrosis** → TB.
Four CXR patterns of TB: **miliary** shadowing, **effusion/empyema**, **cavitation**, **consolidation/collapse**. Name one differential for each.
Extrapulmonary TB map: identify kyphosis/psoas abscess (Pott's), pericardial effusion or constriction, lymph nodes, ascites, meningitis/tuberculoma.
CXR: **bilateral upper-lobe** airspace shadowing with **cavitation** → post-primary pulmonary TB.
Ziehl–Neelsen stain: **red acid-fast bacilli** that kept carbol fuchsin after acid-alcohol washing → mycobacteria.
CT chest: countless small, evenly spread nodules throughout both lungs → **miliary TB**.
Mantoux test: intradermal PPD on the inner forearm, read at 48–72 h; measure **induration across the forearm**, positive at **≥ 5 mm** (Davidson).
IGRA principle: T cells release **IFN-γ** after exposure to MTB-specific antigens; T-SPOT.TB counts spots, QuantiFERON measures IFN-γ by ELISA.
